title: El Niño is now stronger than at any point in the last 1,000 years, study finds
gist: A University of Michigan-led study reconstructed a 1,000-year eastern Pacific ocean temperature record from Galápagos coral cores and found El Niño temperature variability since 1984 is 36.5% higher than the preindustrial era (1000-1850) and 16.2% higher than 1851-1982, a shift climate models attribute to human-caused warming with about 99% confidence, and researchers expect the next El Niño (already developing) to break records.

themes.theme: El Niño is unprecedented in the historical/paleoclimate record

insights.claim: A team led by Julie Cole, an environmental scientist at the University of Michigan, reconstructed a thousand-year eastern Pacific ocean surface temperature record by analyzing strontium-to-calcium ratios and oxygen isotopes in fossilized Galápagos coral cores, finding El Niño events today are more violent than any recorded since roughly 1100 CE.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: This is a rare direct paleoclimate measurement (not a model projection) showing current ENSO behavior is genuinely outside historical bounds, giving investors in agriculture, insurance, and commodities a harder empirical basis for pricing climate-driven weather volatility risk.
insights.quote: It turns out that El Niño in the eastern Pacific has never been as violent as it is now. “The events don’t look anything like what we see in the pre-industrial era,” Cole said.
insights.locator: It turns out that El Niño

insights.claim: ENSO temperature variability since 1984 runs 36.5 percent higher than during the preindustrial period from 1000 to 1850 CE and is still 16.2 percent higher than during the 1851-1982 period, with all three intervals statistically distinct and the trend continuing upward.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified escalation (36.5% and 16.2%) in the dominant driver of year-to-year global climate variability is a hard number investors in weather-sensitive sectors (agriculture, insurance/reinsurance, energy, shipping) can use to model tail risk more aggressively than historical baselines suggest.
insights.quote: Temperature variability since 1984 runs 36.5 percent higher than it was during the preindustrial stretch from 1000 to 1850 CE and is still 16.2 percent higher than during the period from 1851 to 1982.

insights.claim: El Niño events that once ran one to two degrees above normal temperature in the Galápagos now run three to four degrees above normal, and the record shows a shift toward positive skewness, meaning it is specifically the warm El Niño phase (not the cool La Niña phase) that has intensified.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The asymmetric intensification (warm phase strengthening more than cold phase) means downstream impacts like Peru flooding, Australian drought, and global commodity/crop disruptions tied specifically to strong El Niño years are the more probable escalating risk to model, versus La Niña-driven effects.
insights.quote: The skewness turned positive,” Cole said, “and the positive skewness indicates that it’s the warmer events that got stronger.
insights.locator: The corals also record a shift

insights.claim: Neither the Little Ice Age nor the Medieval Warm Period left a comparable fingerprint on ENSO variability in the coral record, indicating the current intensification is not simply a natural climate cycle repeating a past pattern.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Ruling out precedent from two well-known past climate anomalies strengthens the case that today's El Niño intensification is a novel phenomenon tied to modern warming rather than a recurring natural pattern, reducing the odds this reverses on its own.
insights.quote: Neither the Little Ice Age nor the Medieval warm period left such a distinct fingerprint on ENSO variability.
insights.locator: The extra variability in our times

insights.claim: To test whether human-caused warming (not natural ENSO noise) explains the intensification, researchers compared the coral record against climate model simulations that included only natural factors like volcanoes and solar variability (excluding greenhouse gas changes), and found none of those natural-only simulations reproduced a swing as large as what actually occurred, with the observed increase falling outside model-internal variability at a confidence level approaching 99 percent.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A ~99% confidence attribution to human-caused (not natural) forcing is a strong scientific basis for treating stronger El Niño events as a structural, worsening climate-risk trend rather than random variability -- material for anyone pricing long-duration climate risk (insurance, agriculture, infrastructure).
insights.quote: The actual increase retrieved from coral records sits outside the models’ internal variability at a confidence level approaching 99 percent. The team interpreted this as evidence that what’s currently happening with ENSO would not be happening without us.

insights.claim: The intensification signal is clearer in the eastern Pacific (near the Galápagos) than in the central Pacific (Line Islands corals), which is consistent with climate models predicting that a human-caused ENSO increase should emerge first in the eastern Pacific.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The geographic pattern matching model predictions (east before central Pacific) adds independent corroboration to the human-attribution finding, strengthening confidence the trend will continue to spread and intensify.
insights.quote: A forced, human-caused increase should appear first in the east. “The faster emergence in the eastern Pacific is exactly consistent with the models,” Cole said.
insights.locator: But an ambiguous central Pacific coral record

insights.claim: Global warming is already expected to intensify ENSO's hydrological consequences (wetter wet phases, drier dry ones) simply because a hotter atmosphere holds more water vapor, regardless of whether ENSO's own temperature swings are also strengthening -- and if both effects are occurring together, their impacts compound.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: This is a two-factor risk model (stronger temperature swings PLUS a wetter/drier hydrological amplifier) that investors in agriculture, water infrastructure, and disaster/reinsurance markets should use to think about compounding, not merely additive, future climate volatility.
insights.quote: But if ENSO temperature swings are strengthening too, the effects compound.
insights.locator: Global warming is already expected to intensify

insights.claim: Two strong El Niño events have occurred since the study's coral data period ended, and researchers including Cole expect a currently developing El Niño to break records, which Cole says confirms the intensification trend is not a one-off fluke but represents a new, more extreme style of El Niño going forward.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A record-breaking El Niño being actively forecast right now (as of this article) is a near-term, trackable event -- investors in commodities (coffee, cocoa, grains), energy demand, and insurance losses tied to El Niño years should watch its development closely as a live catalyst.
insights.quote: Two more strong El Niño events have arrived since the end of the team’s coral temperature logs, with another developing now that Cole (and most other experts) expects to break records. “It suggests that what we see is not a fluke,” she said, “but rather a new type of situation for El Niño, a new style of El Niño.”
insights.locator: The future, though, has already started happening

insights.claim: Cole and colleagues attribute the intensification of El Niño directly to warming caused by fossil fuel use, stating the root cause is not ambiguous even though the future magnitude and character of further change remains uncertain.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A named climate scientist stating unambiguous attribution to fossil fuel use in a peer-reviewed Science study adds to the body of evidence linking specific, quantifiable extreme-weather risk to continued fossil fuel consumption, relevant to energy-transition and climate-liability discussions.
insights.quote: We are attributing that to warming, and we know what causes the warming, and it’s our use of fossil fuels,” Cole said. “One more warning sign here of what we’re facing in a warmer world.
